citations.quote:
A Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with numbered input nodes,
constant nodes, and gates from the fixed basis $\{\mathsf{AND},\mathsf{OR},\mathsf{NOT}\}$;
AND and OR gates have two predecessors, NOT gates have one, and constants
have values zero or one. Its output is one designated node. A family
$(C_n)_{n\ge0}$ has exactly $n$ input nodes labeled $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ in
$C_n$ and polynomially many nodes as a function of $n+2$. The family is
**logspace-uniform** when a deterministic read-only-input logspace transducer,
on input $1^n$ and a query with binary node indices of length $O(\log(n+2))$,
halts and answers the size, gate-type (including input labels and constant
values), and predecessor queries for the
topologically numbered encoding of $C_n$, and answers which numbered gate is
the designated output. In particular, it can stream that polynomial-length
encoding without storing it.

derivations.claim: Fix one valid query to the indexed transducer. Its read-only input and query tapes have polynomially many head positions in $n$, its work tapes use $O(\log(n+2))$ cells over a fixed alphabet, and its finite control has finitely many states. Thus it has at most $(n+2)^c$ internal configurations for some fixed $c$. A halting deterministic computation cannot repeat an internal configuration: because the input tapes are read-only and the output tape is write-only, a repetition would repeat the same future transitions forever. Hence each size, type, predecessor, or output query takes polynomial time and writes polynomially many bits.

Query the size once, then query the type and the required predecessor indices of each of the at most $q(n)$ nodes and query the designated output. This uses polynomially many queries, each of polynomial time by step 1.1. Every node index is at most $n+q(n)$, so each self-delimiting index has $O(\log(n+q(n)+2))$ bits. Writing the header and all records therefore takes polynomial time and produces a polynomial-length full list.

Each record is the exact gate type and predecessor data returned for that same topological node, and the final output field is the exact designated node. The full-list decoder consequently evaluates the same ordered DAG on every input, including the case $n=0$ when the input list is empty.

citations.quote: Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space, let $K$ be a finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space, and let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty outcome set. A **finite instrument** from $H$ to $K$ is a family of complex-linear maps $\mathcal I_a:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$, one for each $a\in\Omega$, such that each $\mathcal I_a$ is completely positive ([[def-qc-completely-positive-map]]) and

The map $\Phi$ is **completely positive** if, for every finite $r\ge1$, $\Phi^{(r)}$ sends every nonnegative operator on $H\otimes R$ to a nonnegative operator on $K\otimes R$ ([[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]). The quantifier includes $r=1$; complete positivity therefore implies positivity. No Kraus, Choi, or Stinespring characterization is part of this definition.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The operator $T$ is **non-negative** when $T$ is
self-adjoint in the sense of [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]] and

For every $d\ge1$, the ordered computational basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of
the register $Q_d$ from [[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]] is an
orthonormal basis for its declared inner product. In particular, the
one-dimensional zero-qubit register has the basis $\{1\}$.

Let $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$ be a finite ordered list of finite-dimensional
complex inner-product spaces with specified ordered orthonormal bases of
sizes $d_0,\ldots,d_{n-1}$, allowing $d_k=0$. The elementary tensors of the
factor bases, ordered lexicographically, form an orthonormal basis of the
tensor register, and
For $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and $B\in M_{n\times m}(F)$,

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, with the root library's convention that the inner product is linear in its first argument. A **density operator** on $H$ is a non-negative endomorphism $\rho:H\to H$ with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$; non-negative and trace have the meanings of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]] and [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. The zero-dimensional space is excluded: its only endomorphism has trace $0$.

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For $n=0$, the tensor map is the identity map $z\mapsto z$ on the empty tensor
product $\mathbb C$.

derivations.claim: Each basis projection $P_a$ and $Q_b$ is diagonal with entries $0$ or $1$, hence self-adjoint and idempotent; distinct projections in each family are orthogonal and each family sums to the identity. By [F8], their lifted maps $P_a\otimes I_B$ and $I_A\otimes Q_b$ are self-adjoint idempotents, and each lifted family sums to $I_{A\otimes B}$.

The product basis $(e_a\otimes g_b)_{a,b}$ is orthonormal by [F4]. Therefore the coordinates of $\psi$ satisfy $\sum_{a,b}|c_{a,b}|^2=1$. By [F7], $\rho=|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|$ has matrix $v v^\dagger$, so for every coordinate vector $u$ its quadratic form is $u^\dagger v v^\dagger u=|v^\dagger u|^2\ge0$ and its trace is $\sum_{a,b}|c_{a,b}|^2=1$. Hence $\rho$ is a density operator by [F6].

Each branch map is complex-linear. For any finite reference register $R$, write an operator $Q$ on $(A\otimes B)\otimes R$ in the ancilla blocks of [F2]. Its amplified branch sends each block $Q_{ij}$ to $CQ_{ij}C$, so [F8] identifies the full block matrix as $Q'=(C\otimes I_R)Q(C\otimes I_R)$, where $C$ is the lifted projector from step 1.1. If $Q$ is nonnegative, then $Q'$ is self-adjoint and $\langle Q'u,u\rangle=\langle Q(C\otimes I_R)u,(C\otimes I_R)u\rangle\ge0$ for every $u$ by [F3], so every amplification preserves nonnegative operators. Thus each branch is completely positive by [F2].

Write $v$ for the coordinate column of $\psi$ and $C$ for either lifted projector. By [F7], the corresponding branch is $Cvv^\dagger C=(Cv)(Cv)^\dagger$. For outcome $a$, $(P_a\otimes I_B)\psi=\sum_b c_{a,b}e_a\otimes g_b$, so the branch matrix has diagonal entries $|c_{a,b}|^2$ on coordinates $(a,b)$ and zero elsewhere; its trace is $\sum_b|c_{a,b}|^2$. For outcome $b$, $(I_A\otimes Q_b)\psi=\sum_a c_{a,b}e_a\otimes g_b$, so its branch matrix has diagonal entries $|c_{a,b}|^2$ on coordinates $(a,b)$ and zero elsewhere; its trace is $\sum_a|c_{a,b}|^2$. These traces are the asserted probabilities by [F1].

For every operator $R$, cyclicity of trace and idempotence give $\sum_a\operatorname{tr}((P_a\otimes I_B)R(P_a\otimes I_B)) =\operatorname{tr}\!\left(R\sum_a(P_a\otimes I_B)\right) =\operatorname{tr}(R).$ The same calculation gives $\sum_b\operatorname{tr}((I_A\otimes Q_b)R(I_A\otimes Q_b))=\operatorname{tr}(R)$. Together with step 2.1 these are the finite-instrument conditions of [F1].

If a branch vector $w=C\psi$ has positive probability $p=\sum_i|w_i|^2$ from step 2.2, its conditional operator in [F1] is $|(w/\sqrt p)\rangle\langle(w/\sqrt p)|$. Its coordinate quadratic form is nonnegative and its trace is $\sum_i|w_i|^2/p=1$, so it is a density operator by [F6]–[F7]; a zero-probability branch has no conditional state by [F1].

citations.quote:
1. Allocate one fresh clean value bit $w_v$ for each non-input node $v$.
2. Process nodes in the supplied order. Leave a constant-$0$ bit untouched; apply $X$ to a constant-$1$ bit. For a NOT node with input wire $u$, apply $X(w_v)$ then $\operatorname{CNOT}_{u\to w_v}$. For an AND node with inputs $u,v$, apply $T(u,v,w_v)$. For an OR node, apply $\operatorname{CNOT}_{u\to w_v}$, then $\operatorname{CNOT}_{v\to w_v}$, then $T(u,v,w_v)$. If a two-port node uses the same source identifier twice, first allocate a fresh clean scratch bit $s$, copy the source into $s$ by CNOT, use the distinct physical wires as the gate inputs, and uncopy $s$ immediately after writing $w_v$.
3. For each output port $j$, apply CNOT from its named input or value wire to target bit $y_j$.
4. Append the inverse of the entire node-evaluation list in reverse chronological order, including the temporary source-copy and uncopy instructions. Return the resulting finite gate list, with the input register unchanged and the target changed only by the stated XOR into $y$.

Let $n,m\ge0$, $x\in\{0,1\}^n$, and $y\in\{0,1\}^m$. Let a finite topologically ordered Boolean DAG have $S$ non-input nodes, including constants, and $E$ input-port uses counted with multiplicity. Its gates are NOT, AND, OR, and constants, with fan-in at most two, and it has $m$ ordered output ports computing $f(x)$. Under the fixed elementary alphabet in [[def-qc-elementary-circuit-resources]], counting each occurrence of $X$, CNOT, and Toffoli as one gate and one serial layer, [[alg-qc-reversible-embedding]] returns a circuit on the ordered input, target, and work registers implementing
$$
|x,y,0^w\rangle\longmapsto|x,y\oplus f(x),0^w\rangle
$$
for every basis input $x$ and every target string $y$. It uses at most $6S+4E+m$ elementary gate occurrences, at most $S+E$ clean work bits, and serial depth at most $6S+4E+m$. The same operator action holds coherently on arbitrary superpositions and after adjoining any finite reference register.

Write $S=T^2=\operatorname{diag}(1,i)$ and
$Z=T^4=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$. Pauli $X,Y,Z$ are as in
[[def-qc-pauli-matrices]]. On two ordered wires,
$\operatorname{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,b\mathbin\oplus a\rangle$; the first wire
is control and the second target. A circuit is a finite chronological word of
these gates at stated wire positions; its matrix is the product with later
gates on the left. No extra wire or controlled-$T$ operation is implicit.

A gate occurrence on the $n$ wires is a pair $(g,(w_0,\ldots,w_{r(g)-1}))$ with distinct wire labels $w_j\in[n]$; the tuple order is the input and output factor order of the local gate. A layer is a finite ordered list of gate occurrences whose wire supports are pairwise disjoint. A unitary circuit is a finite chronological list $L_1,\ldots,L_d$ of such layers, with $L_1$ applied first and $L_d$ last; $d=0$ is the empty circuit. Its input, output, and terminally measured wires are specified as ordered lists without repetitions in $[n]$. This syntax specifies finite data only; the semantic action of gates on the full register is defined separately.

For a gate occurrence $g=(\gamma,w)$ in a circuit on $\mathcal Q_n$, let $\widetilde U_g$ be the global embedding from [[lem-qc-local-gate-wire-embedding]]. For a layer $L_t=(g_1,\ldots,g_s)$, define
$$U_{L_t}:=\widetilde U_{g_s}\cdots\widetilde U_{g_1}.$$
For a circuit with chronological layers $L_1,\ldots,L_d$, define
$$U_C:=U_{L_d}\cdots U_{L_1}.$$
The empty circuit and every empty layer denote the identity on $\mathcal Q_n$.

The following fixed-order code makes the full circuit and its designated input/output wires effective. A unary natural $r\in\mathbb N$ is written $1^r0$, including the one-symbol code $0$ for $r=0$. A self-delimiting binary natural $r$ is written $1^{|\operatorname{bin}(r)|}0\operatorname{bin}(r)$, where $\operatorname{bin}(r)$ is its ordinary binary numeral with no leading zeros and $\operatorname{bin}(0)=0$. The header gives the input-wire count $n$ and total wire count $m$ in unary, followed by the gate count $g$ as a self-delimiting natural; validity requires $m\ge n$.

derivations.claim: For $a,b,c\in\{0,1\}$ set $d=a+b+c-(a\oplus b)-(a\oplus c)-(b\oplus c)+(a\oplus b\oplus c)$, with ordinary integer addition and subtraction. If exactly $k$ of $a,b,c$ equal $1$, then $d=0$ for $k=0,1,2$ and $d=4$ for $k=3$. Thus $d=4abc$.

Use one clean scratch bit $r$. Apply $T$ to each of the three data bits. For each of the three pair parities, compute that XOR into $r$ with two CNOTs, apply $T^\dagger$ to $r$, and undo the same two CNOTs. Compute $a\oplus b\oplus c$ into $r$ with three CNOTs, apply $T$, and undo those three CNOTs. Each parity routine restores $r$ to zero and leaves the data bits unchanged. The total phase on $|a,b,c\rangle$ is $\omega^d=(-1)^{abc}$, so this circuit is CCZ; it uses seven $T$ or $T^\dagger$ gates and eighteen CNOTs.

Conjugate this CCZ circuit by $H$ on the third data wire. If $ab=0$, CCZ is the identity on that wire; if $ab=1$, it applies $Z=T^4$, and direct multiplication of the displayed matrices gives $HZH=X$. The result is therefore $|a,b,c\rangle\mapsto|a,b,c\oplus ab\rangle$, the Toffoli action. The scratch wire is still zero, and the replacement uses $2+7+18=27$ QC14 gates.
Replace each $X$ in the reversible embedding by $HT^4H$, which equals $X$ because $T^4=Z$ and $HZH=X$; this uses six QC14 gates. Leave each CNOT unchanged and replace each Toffoli by step 3.1.

By [F2], the original macro list has at most $6S+4E+m$ occurrences. Each macro replacement has the same action on its data wires, returns the added scratch to zero, and uses at most $27$ gates, so the compiled list has at most $27(6S+4E+m)$ gates and at most $S+E+1$ clean work wires. The exact matrix identity on every computational-basis input extends by linearity to superpositions.

Traverse the explicit topological DAG once to produce the finite macro list of [F1], then replace each macro by its fixed gate sequence and fixed scratch-wire indices. The traversal and each replacement emit a constant number of records per node, port use, or output; every encoded wire index has $O(\log(n+S+E+m+2))$ bits. The unary wire header and all self-delimiting records in [F5] consequently have polynomial total length and can be written in polynomial time. The ordered input, target, work and output indices satisfy [F4]–[F5], so this is a valid QC14 full-list circuit with the action established in step 5.1.

citations.quote: A **promise problem** is a pair $(Y,N)$ of disjoint subsets of $\{0,1\}^*$. Its promise is $Y\cup N$. A deterministic solver must accept every word of $Y$ and reject every word of $N$, with either answer allowed elsewhere. The pair belongs to $\mathrm{PromiseP}$ if such a solver has a polynomial time bound on every input.

For every fixed deterministic Turing machine $M$ that halts in polynomial
time, there is a polynomial-size logspace-uniform Boolean circuit family
$(C_n)$ such that $C_n(x)=1$ exactly when $M$ accepts
$x\in\{0,1\}^n$.

Let $(C_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a polynomial-size Boolean circuit family generated in the indexed-gate, logspace sense of [[def-logspace-uniform-circuit-family]]. Assume a fixed polynomial $q$ bounds the number of non-input nodes of $C_n$ by $q(n)$. There is one deterministic polynomial-time machine which, on unary input $1^n$, writes a complete self-delimiting topological gate list for $C_n$, including its input count, all node records and its designated output. The resulting list describes the same circuit and therefore computes the same Boolean function.

where $f(x)$ is the ordered Boolean output. It uses at most $27(6S+4E+m)$ QC14 gate occurrences, and the full self-delimiting circuit list is produced in time polynomial in the Boolean-DAG description length. The same action holds on superpositions by linearity.

A promise problem $\Pi=(Y,N)$ belongs to $\mathrm{EQP}$ in the QC14 model if there is a full-list uniform family $(C_n)_{n\ge0}$ and a polynomial-time total acceptance predicate $A_n$ as in [[def-qc-promise-computation-model]], [[def-qc-uniform-circuit-family]], and [[def-qc-quantum-acceptance-probability]], using the exact gate and cost conventions of [[def-qc-circuit-cost-model]] and [[def-qc-clifford-t-gate-library]], such that

In this page, $\mathrm{ZQP}$ denotes the following bounded-failure zero-error promise class. A promise problem $\Pi=(Y,N)$ belongs to $\mathrm{ZQP}$ if there are a full-list uniform QC14 family $(C_n)$, a polynomial-time total label decoder $D_n(x,z)\in\{\mathrm{YES},\mathrm{NO},?\}$, and the finite output law of [[def-qc-promise-computation-model]], [[def-qc-uniform-circuit-family]], and [[def-qc-quantum-acceptance-probability]], such that for every $x\in Y$ the probability of $\mathrm{YES}$ is at least $2/3$ and the probability of $\mathrm{NO}$ is zero, while for every $x\in N$ the probability of $\mathrm{NO}$ is at least $2/3$ and the probability of $\mathrm{YES}$ is zero. All output strings receive one of the three labels, so the remaining probability is the allowed failure label $?$; the output law is normalized by [[thm-qc-output-acceptance-law-normalizes]]. No promise condition is imposed off $Y\cup N$.

A promise problem $\Pi=(Y,N)$ belongs to **BQP in the QC14 model** when there exist a full-list uniform family $(C_n)$ and a polynomial-time acceptance predicate $A_n$ as in [[def-qc-uniform-circuit-family]] and [[def-qc-quantum-acceptance-probability]] such that, for every $x\in Y$,
$$p_{C_{|x|}}(x)\ge\frac23,$$
and for every $x\in N$,
$$p_{C_{|x|}}(x)\le\frac13.$$
By [[thm-qc-output-acceptance-law-normalizes]], $p_{C_n}(x)$ is the probability of the specified acceptance event and lies in $[0,1]$. No condition is imposed for $x\notin Y\cup N$ ([[def-promise-problem]]). The gate alphabet is exactly $H,T,T^\dagger,\mathrm{CNOT}$; its matrix entries lie in $\mathbb Q(\zeta_8)=\mathbb Q(i,\sqrt2)$ as specified by [[def-qc-uniform-circuit-family]]. This definition does not assert a BQP-versus-classical separation, nor does it assert an unproved equivalence with another circuit-uniformity convention.

For every finite promise computation, every length $n$, and every classical input $x\in\{0,1\}^n$, the output weights $p_{C_n}(z\mid x)$ from [[def-qc-quantum-acceptance-probability]] are nonnegative and sum to one over $z\in\{0,1\}^{|O_n|}$. The acceptance probability is the probability of the event $\{z:A_n(x,z)=1\}$, lies in $[0,1]$, and agrees with the finite computational-basis POVM outcome law on the named output register.

derivations.claim: Let $\Pi=(Y,N)\in\mathrm{PromiseP}$ and choose its deterministic polynomial-time decider $M$ from [F1]. The Boolean circuit family of [F2] computes $M$; [F3] gives a polynomial-time full-list generator, and [F4] compiles each list into a QC14 family whose one-bit target is $1$ exactly when $M$ accepts. Use the target bit as the acceptance predicate. For every $x\in Y$ the acceptance probability is $1$, and for every $x\in N$ it is $0$, so $\Pi\in\mathrm{EQP}$.

If $\Pi\in\mathrm{EQP}$, take its witnessing family and define $D_n(x,z)=\mathrm{YES}$ when its acceptance predicate accepts and $D_n(x,z)=\mathrm{NO}$ otherwise. This is a total polynomial-time decoder. The exact probabilities in [F5] make the wrong definite label have probability zero and the correct definite label have probability one on each promised side; therefore the same family witnesses $\Pi\in\mathrm{ZQP}$.

If $\Pi\in\mathrm{ZQP}$, keep its full-list family and define the BQP acceptance predicate to accept exactly when $D_n(x,z)=\mathrm{YES}$. On $Y$ this event has probability at least $2/3$. On $N$ it has probability zero, since a wrong definite YES label is forbidden. By [F8] these event probabilities are normalized, and [F7] gives $\Pi\in\mathrm{BQP}$.

derivations.claim: If $\Pi\in\mathrm{PromiseP}$, run its deterministic decider as a PTM that ignores all random bits. Its acceptance probability is $1$ on $Y$ and $0$ on $N$, so it satisfies [F2]. Thus $\mathrm{PromiseP}\subseteq\mathrm{PromiseBPP}$.

Now let $\Pi\in\mathrm{PromiseBPP}$ be witnessed by a PTM $M$. Choose a strictly increasing positive integer polynomial $R(n)$ that bounds both its run time and the number of fair bits it can use on length-$n$ inputs. By [F3], using a uniform $R(n)$-bit string and ignoring its unused suffix preserves every acceptance probability.

For a binary word $w$ of length $m$, define one deterministic polynomial-time machine $M^\sharp$ as follows. Search for an $n$ with $m=n+R(n)$; strict increase makes it unique if it exists. If none exists, output $0$. If it exists, split $w=x\|r$ with $|x|=n$ and $|r|=R(n)$, simulate $M$ on $x$ using $r$ as its fair random tape, and output its accept bit. The search and simulation take polynomial time in $m$, since $n\le m$ and $R$ is a fixed polynomial.

Apply [F4] to $M^\sharp$, then [F5] to emit the Boolean gate list at length $m(n)=n+R(n)$. Compose this generator with the polynomial-time map $n\mapsto m(n)$. Apply [F6] to that list. In the resulting QC14 family on input $x$, designate the next $R(n)$ auxiliary wires as the random register, apply $H$ to each from its initial zero state, and then run the reversible compiler on the $x$ and random registers with a zero target and clean work. The generator adds the $R(n)$ Hadamards, changes the header's input count to $n$, and retains the same total wires, target, and compiled gate records. All these list operations take polynomial time in $n$.

By [F8]–[F9], the Hadamards prepare $2^{-R(n)/2}\sum_{r\in\{0,1\}^{R(n)}}|r\rangle$ on the zero-initialized random register. For each basis $r$, the reversible circuit writes exactly the bit $M(x;r)$ into the target and returns its work to zero. Distinct $r$ values remain in orthogonal computational-basis states of the unmeasured random register. Therefore, by [F10], the target's acceptance probability is $2^{-R(n)}\#\{r\in\{0,1\}^{R(n)}:M(x;r)\text{ accepts}\},$ which is exactly the PTM acceptance probability in [F3]. Its YES and NO bounds in [F2] are the BQP bounds in [F7]. Hence $\mathrm{PromiseBPP}\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}$.

For an ordinary language $L\in\mathrm{BPP}$, use the total promise pair $(L,\{0,1\}^*\setminus L)$. Its BPP PTM satisfies the PromiseBPP definition [F2], so step 4.1 gives a BQP family for the language. Thus $\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}$.

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

In a finite probability space $(\Omega,w)$, events $A\subseteq B\subseteq\Omega$ satisfy
$$0\le\mathbb P(A)\le\mathbb P(B)\le1,$$
and
$$\mathbb P(\varnothing)=0,\qquad \mathbb P(\Omega)=1,\qquad \mathbb P(A^c)=1-\mathbb P(A),\qquad \mathbb P(B\setminus A)=\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A).$$
Probability zero need not imply that an event is empty.

derivations.claim: Consider the finite input distribution that chooses YES or NO with probability $1/2$. In the YES case choose a uniform permutation of $V_n$. In the NO case choose a uniform nonzero mask $s$, then a uniform injection from the $N/2$ cosets $\{x,x\oplus s\}$ into the $N$ output labels. Every valid NO function has a unique mask, and each mask has the same number of such injections, so this is uniform over valid NO functions.

It suffices to bound every deterministic query strategy: any randomized strategy has finitely many possible histories and actions up to depth $T$, so its conditional action choices can be represented as a finite distribution over deterministic decision trees. Repeated queries can be removed by caching their earlier answer, so assume every queried address is fresh.

Fix a deterministic strategy and a query index $k\le T$. Since $N\ge16$, the premise $T\le\sqrt N/8$ implies $k\le N/2$. Suppose its first $k-1$ distinct query addresses $x_1,\ldots,x_{k-1}$ have produced distinct outputs. Under a NO mask, this transcript is possible exactly when $s\ne x_i\oplus x_j$ for every $i<j<k$. Thus at most $\binom{k-1}{2}$ of the $N-1$ nonzero masks are excluded. For every remaining mask, the queried addresses lie in distinct cosets; the number of injective assignments of output labels to the unqueried cosets is $\frac{(N-k+1)!}{(N/2)!},$ independent of the mask. Hence, conditioned on this transcript, the mask is uniform among at least $N-1-\binom{k-1}{2}$ candidates.

The next address $x_k$ is determined by the transcript. At most $k-1$ candidate masks, namely $x_k\oplus x_j$ for $j<k$, make its output collide with a previous output. Therefore $\Pr[\text{first collision at query }k\mid\text{no earlier collision}] \le \frac{k-1}{N-1-\binom{k-1}{2}}.$ If there is no collision, $x_k$ belongs to a new coset whose output label is uniform among the $N-k+1$ unused labels, exactly as the next output of a uniformly random permutation. Couple the two oracle transcripts to use the same unused label until a Simon collision occurs; the adaptive address choices then also agree up to that time.

For $T\le\sqrt N/8$ and $N\ge16$, each denominator in step 3.1 is at least $N-1-T^2/2>N/2$. Summing the conditional first-collision bounds gives $\Pr_{\mathrm{NO}}[\text{a collision by query }T] \le \sum_{k=2}^T\frac{2(k-1)}N =\frac{T(T-1)}N\le\frac1{64}<\frac13.$ This also bounds the probability that the coupled transcripts differ.

Let $D$ be the deterministic decision bit, with $1$ meaning YES. Under the coupling, its outputs in the two cases differ with probability at most $1/64$, so $\Pr_{\mathrm{YES}}[D=1]-\Pr_{\mathrm{NO}}[D=1]\le\frac1{64}.$ Its average success under the equal mixture is $\frac12\bigl(\Pr_{\mathrm{YES}}[D=1]+\Pr_{\mathrm{NO}}[D=0]\bigr) =\frac12\left(1+\Pr_{\mathrm{YES}}[D=1]-\Pr_{\mathrm{NO}}[D=1]\right) \le\frac{1+1/64}{2}<\frac23.$ By step 1.2 the same bound holds for every randomized algorithm. A worst-case error bound of $1/3$ would imply average success at least $2/3$, a contradiction. Therefore at least $\sqrt N/8$ queries are required for all sufficiently large $n$, which is $\Omega(2^{n/2})$.

derivations.claim: By the factorwise tensor rule [F5], $H^{\otimes n}|x\rangle=N^{-1/2}\sum_{y\in V_n}(-1)^{x\cdot y}|y\rangle$. In particular the first Hadamards prepare $N^{-1/2}\sum_{x\in V_n}|x,0^n\rangle$. After one query the state is $|\psi_f\rangle=N^{-1/2}\sum_{x\in V_n}|x,f(x)\rangle.$ For each function-register result $z$ in the image of $f$, [F4] gives probability $|f^{-1}(z)|/N$ and the conditional input superposition that is uniform on that fiber.

If $f$ is YES, every fiber is a singleton $\{x\}$. The conditional input state is $|x\rangle$, and the second Hadamards give amplitude $N^{-1/2}(-1)^{x\cdot y}$ at every $y\in V_n$. By the first-register instrument law [F4], its squared modulus is the conditional output probability $1/N$, independent of the measured function-register value; hence the unconditional sample is uniform on $V_n$.

If $f$ is NO with mask $s\ne0$, a positive-probability fiber has the form $\{x,x\oplus s\}$. Its conditional input state is $(|x\rangle+|x\oplus s\rangle)/\sqrt2$. After the second Hadamards the amplitude at $y$ is $\frac{(-1)^{x\cdot y}}{\sqrt{2N}}\bigl(1+(-1)^{s\cdot y}\bigr).$ It is zero when $s\cdot y=1$ and has squared modulus $2/N$ when $s\cdot y=0$. By [F4], these squared moduli are the conditional output probabilities. Pairing $y$ with $y\oplus e_j$ for a coordinate $j$ with $s_j=1$ shows that exactly $N/2$ strings lie in $s^\perp$. The conditional law is therefore uniform on $s^\perp$ and independent of the measured fiber label, so the unconditional law is the same.

In the NO case every sample lies in $s^\perp$, which is proper because $e_j\notin s^\perp$ when $s_j=1$. The span of the samples is proper, so its rank is less than $n$ and the algorithm rejects. The elimination procedure preserves row span under row swaps and row XORs; at termination its nonzero rows have distinct pivot columns and are linearly independent. They still span the original rows, so the pivot count is the matrix rank. At most $n$ pivots each inspect and update $O(n+2)$ rows of $n$ bits, giving $O(n^3)$ bit operations.

Each run reinitializes both registers and uses no earlier outcome as an input. Thus the conditional law of the next sample given any previous transcript is the same one-run law; induction on the number of runs gives the product law, and [F7] identifies the coordinates as independent. In the YES case each sample is uniform on $V_n$ by step 2.1. Their matrix has rank below $n$ exactly when some nonzero $t\in V_n$ satisfies $t\cdot y_j=0$ for every row $j$: Gaussian elimination uses invertible row operations and produces fewer than $n$ pivot columns, so a free variable can be set to $1$ and the pivot variables solved backwards to give a nonzero solution of the homogeneous system. Conversely, if such a $t$ exists, every row lies in its kernel; a coordinate vector $e_k$ with $t_k=1$ is outside that kernel, so the rows cannot span $V_n$.

Fix $t\ne0$ and choose $k$ with $t_k=1$. The involution $y\mapsto y\oplus e_k$ pairs vectors with opposite values of $t\cdot y$, so a uniform sample satisfies $t\cdot y=0$ with probability $1/2$. Independence gives probability $2^{-m}$ that all $m$ samples are orthogonal to $t$. Pointwise, the indicator of the union over the $N-1$ nonzero $t$ is at most the sum of their indicators; summing over the finite probability space yields $\Pr[\operatorname{rank}<n]\le (N-1)2^{-m}=(2^n-1)2^{-(n+2)}<\frac14.$ The procedure makes exactly $m=n+2$ oracle calls.
